summary: Faithfulness of explanations has formal concept-level definitions only for input-output explanations: Dasgupta et al.'s consistency and sufficiency, Potyka et al.'s qualitative faithfulness, logic-based abductive explanations, and axiom systems (Sundararajan et al.; Amgoud & Ben-Naim). Impossibility theorems exist for attributions (Bilodeau; Fokkema; Han's no-free-lunch) and for concept bottlenecks (Teso). None defines faithfulness of free-text or CoT reasoning as a property of the generating process: Barez et al. give verbal conditions (soundness, causal relevance, completeness), and Perrier formalizes only soundness. Introspection has semi-formal causal criteria: Comsa & Shanahan (accurate and causally linked), Lindsey (accuracy, counterfactual grounding, internality, metacognitive representation), and Song et al. (more reliable than any equally cheap third-party process). An SCM with path-specific counterfactual conditions, plus Dasgupta-style sufficiency relative to a compute-bounded observer class, could cover faithfulness, introspection, simulatability and monitorability together.

candidates.title: Framework for Evaluating Faithfulness of Local Explanations
candidates.authors: Sanjoy Dasgupta, Nave Frost, Michal Moshkovitz
candidates.formal_object: Faithfulness of an explanation system (f,e) split into consistency (same explanation implies same prediction) and sufficiency (any instance satisfying the explanation gets the same prediction), local and global, w.r.t. a data distribution.
candidates.key_formula: m^c(x)=\Pr_{x'\in_\mu C_\pi}\big(f(x')=f(x)\big),\ C_\pi=\{x\in\mathcal{X}: e(x)=\pi\};\quad m^s(x)=\Pr_{x'\in_\mu C_x}\big(f(x')=f(x)\big),\ C_x=\{x'\in\mathcal{X}: A(x',e(x))\}
candidates.assumptions: Input distribution mu; black-box access to f; 'intelligible' explanations with a checkable applicability relation A(x,pi); judges only outputs, not the internal process.
candidates.relevance: Closest formal concept-level definition of faithfulness that is agnostic to explanation format: a free-text rationale works as pi if A is judgeable. Consistency equals Gibbs-decoder accuracy, which links faithfulness, simulatability and checkability.

candidates.title: Impossibility Theorems for Feature Attribution
candidates.authors: Blair Bilodeau, Natasha Jaques, Pang Wei Koh, Been Kim
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(2)
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: hypothesis testing over model classes (statistical decision theory)
candidates.formal_object: Theorems: for moderately rich model classes, any complete and linear attribution method (IG, SHAP) can provably fail to beat random guessing at end-tasks such as local behaviour, spurious features and recourse.
candidates.assumptions: Attribution is complete and linear; model class rich enough (satisfied by neural nets); end-task framed as a hypothesis test about model behaviour.
candidates.relevance: Shows faithfulness is only well defined relative to a concrete end-task or inference. Suggests defining CoT faithfulness by what an observer can correctly infer about behaviour, not by axioms on the explanation.

candidates.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
candidates.formalism: semi-formal interventionist causal criteria (tested by concept injection)
candidates.formal_object: Introspective awareness: a self-report that is accurate, grounded (causally depends on the described state), internal (the influence does not route through sampled outputs) and drawn from a metacognitive representation of the state.
candidates.assumptions: White-box access; the internal state must be identifiable and intervenable (e.g. as an injected concept vector); the metacognitive-representation criterion is not operationalized.
candidates.relevance: Grounding is counterfactual dependence ('if the internal state were different, the description would change accordingly'), and internality is a path-specific condition excluding paths through generated tokens. Both translate directly into SCM or Halpern-Pearl terms.

candidates.title: Privileged Self-Access Matters for Introspection in AI
candidates.authors: Siyuan Song, Harvey Lederman, Jennifer Hu, Kyle Mahowald
candidates.formalism: semi-formal, resource-bounded comparison with third-party observers
candidates.formal_object: Introspection: any process yielding information about internal states that is more reliable than any process of equal or lower computational cost available to a third party.
candidates.assumptions: A reliability measure, a ground-truth internal state, and a class of third-party processes bounded by computational cost.
candidates.relevance: Makes introspection relative to a compute-bounded observer class, the same structure as usable (V-)information and monitor-relative monitorability. It is a natural bridge to formalize introspection and monitorability in one framework. Lindsey endorses it over the lightweight definition.

candidates.title: Logic-Based Explainability in Machine Learning
candidates.venue: Reasoning Web 2022 lecture notes (per Semantic Scholar); arXiv 2211.00541
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: propositional and first-order logic (prime implicants, abduction, minimal hitting sets)
candidates.formal_object: Abductive explanation (AXp): a subset-minimal feature set whose fixed values logically entail the prediction. Its dual is the contrastive explanation (CXp); AXps and CXps are minimal hitting sets of each other.
candidates.assumptions: Exact logical encoding of the classifier kappa; discrete or encodable features; full model access; computing explanations is intractable for large networks.
candidates.relevance: Gives the rigorous notion of a correct (sound) explanation as entailment, and states non-formal explanations' failure as consistency with different predictions. The sufficient/contrastive duality parallels Halpern-Pearl sufficiency and counterfactual causes; usable on an abstracted causal model of the reasoning.

candidates.title: Towards a Theory of Faithfulness: Faithful Explanations of Differentiable Classifiers over Continuous Data
candidates.authors: Nico Potyka, Xiang Yin, Francesca Toni
candidates.formal_object: Qualitative faithfulness: an attribution's sign matches the local direction of the feature's effect. Quantitative faithfulness: magnitudes are proportional to output change. Theorem: every qualitatively faithful method is qualitatively equivalent to gradient scores.
candidates.assumptions: Continuous inputs, differentiable classifier, feature-attribution explanations; local vs global variants.
candidates.relevance: One of the few papers that defines faithfulness itself (not a metric) and proves which explanations can satisfy it. A template for stating local versus global faithfulness and proving characterization results.

candidates.title: Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?
candidates.formal_object: Lightweight introspection: an LLM self-report is introspective if it accurately describes an internal state or mechanism of the LLM through a causal process linking that state and the report.
candidates.assumptions: A ground-truth internal state or mechanism and a notion of causal linkage; no privileged-access or internality requirement.
candidates.relevance: Minimal causal definition (accuracy plus causal connection) that Lindsey and Song et al. build on and criticize. Reads directly as 'the state is an actual cause of a true report', a ready starting point for a Halpern-Pearl formalization.

candidates.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
candidates.authors: Mukund Sundararajan, Ankur Taly, Qiqi Yan
candidates.formal_object: Axioms an attribution method should satisfy: Sensitivity, Implementation Invariance and Completeness (attributions sum to the output difference from a baseline). Integrated Gradients satisfies them.
candidates.assumptions: Differentiable model, a baseline input x', feature-level attributions.
candidates.relevance: Canonical axiomatic approach. Implementation Invariance makes attributions a function of input-output behaviour alone, so axioms of this kind cannot capture process faithfulness of CoT. Its 'completeness' differs from a CoT disclosing all causal factors.

candidates.title: On the (In)fidelity and Sensitivity for Explanations
candidates.authors: Chih-Kuan Yeh, Cheng-Yu Hsieh, Arun Sai Suggala, David I. Inouye, Pradeep Ravikumar
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formalism: probability (expected squared error under a perturbation distribution)
candidates.formal_object: Explanation infidelity: expected squared gap between the output change predicted by the explanation and the actual change under perturbations I drawn from mu_I. Includes optimal explanations and the companion max-sensitivity.
candidates.assumptions: Real-valued model output; a chosen distribution of 'meaningful' perturbations; linear explanation functional.
candidates.relevance: Presented as the definition of (in)fidelity. Makes explicit that faithfulness is relative to a chosen intervention distribution, a parameter any causal definition of CoT faithfulness must also fix.

candidates.title: Axiomatic Foundations of Explainability
candidates.formal_object: Axioms for global class explainers (Success, Irreducibility, Feasibility, Coherence, Coreness, Exhaustivity, Completeness...). Coreness and Exhaustivity are incompatible, which separates sufficient-reason from necessary-reason explainers. Anchors/LIME abstractions violate the axiom that prevents incorrect explanations.
candidates.key_formula: \forall L\in F(Q),\ \forall I\in \mathrm{Inst}_T \text{ s.t. } L\subseteq I,\ I\in \mathrm{Inst}_T^{R}(x)
candidates.assumptions: Finite feature theory, classifier as a function over instances, explanations as sets of literals.
candidates.relevance: Axiomatic, impossibility-bearing account of what an explanation must satisfy. Its split between sufficient and necessary reasons corresponds to the soundness and completeness directions a faithful CoT must have.

candidates.title: Which Explanation Should I Choose? A Function Approximation Perspective to Characterizing Post Hoc Explanations
candidates.authors: Tessa Han, Suraj Srinivas, Himabindu Lakkaraju
candidates.formal_object: Eight attribution methods unified as local function approximation, differing only in neighbourhood and loss. Faithfulness is approximation quality over the neighbourhood. No-free-lunch theorem: no method is optimal across all neighbourhoods.
candidates.assumptions: Explanations are local surrogate models; a neighbourhood distribution and a loss are specified.
candidates.relevance: A unifying framework plus an impossibility result: faithfulness is indexed by the neighbourhood (set of counterfactual inputs). A CoT definition must also say over which interventions it is faithful.

candidates.title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
candidates.authors: Fazl Barez, Tung-Yu Wu, Ivan Arcuschin, Michael Lan, Vincent Wang, Noah Siegel, Nicolas Collignon, Clement Neo, Isabelle Lee, Alasdair Paren, Adel Bibi, Robert Trager, Damiano Fornasiere, John Yan, Yanai Elazar, Yoshua Bengio
candidates.formal_object: A CoT is faithful if it is procedurally sound, causally relevant (negating a step must change the answer, else the step is irrelevant) and complete (discloses all relevant causal aspects), i.e. correct and reflecting the decision process.
candidates.assumptions: A normative standard of correct reasoning; ability to intervene on CoT steps (negation); a notion of the model's 'relevant causal aspects'.
candidates.relevance: The most explicit concept-level specification of CoT faithfulness among the seeds. Its three conditions (soundness, necessity under negation, completeness) are the natural targets for a Halpern-Pearl formalization; semi-formal only.

candidates.title: When Are Concept Bottleneck Model Explanations Faithful and Compact?
candidates.authors: Stefano Teso, Emanuele Marconato, Steve Azzolin, Antonio Vergari
candidates.formal_object: Faithful concept-bottleneck explanation: one that does not misreport which concepts actually matter, in the formal-explainability sense. Theorem: for widespread CBM architectures, faithful explanations must include all bottleneck concepts.
candidates.assumptions: Model factorizes through a concept bottleneck; concepts as logits or random variables; formal (sufficient-reason) explanations.
candidates.relevance: A CoT can be read as a textual bottleneck between input and answer. This impossibility-style result says when compact faithful explanations of bottleneck models exist, and bears on whether a CoT can be both short and complete.

candidates.title: Attribution-based Explanations that Provide Recourse Cannot be Robust
candidates.authors: Hidde Fokkema, Rianne de Heide, Tim van Erven
candidates.venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research (per Semantic Scholar); arXiv 2205.15834
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
candidates.formal_object: Recourse sensitivity, defined via a user utility function, for local attributions and counterfactual explanations. Theorem: no single attribution method can be both recourse-sensitive and robust in general.
candidates.assumptions: Local attribution or counterfactual explanations; a utility over decision changes; continuity/robustness notion on inputs.
candidates.relevance: Impossibility result showing that counterfactual informativeness and stability of explanations trade off. Warns that a definition demanding both counterfactual faithfulness and robustness of rationales may be unsatisfiable.

candidates.title: Typed Chain-of-Thought: A Curry-Howard Framework for Verifying LLM Reasoning
candidates.formal_object: A faithful reasoning trace is analogous to a well-typed program: each CoT step maps to a typed inference, and a successful mapping is a certificate of 'computational faithfulness'.
candidates.assumptions: CoT steps can be extracted and mapped to a typed proof structure; a type system for the domain.
candidates.relevance: One of the few formal criteria stated directly for CoT. It formalizes procedural soundness and checkability, not causal faithfulness to the model's computation, which shows that the two are distinct.

gaps: Faithfulness of free-text or CoT explanations as a property of the generating process: no formal definition in XAI theory; formal definitions cover attributions, rules and sufficient reasons over inputs, and CoT work gives only verbal conditions (Barez et al.) or soundness (Perrier).
Completeness of a CoT (disclosing all causally relevant factors): no formal definition; attribution 'completeness' (Sundararajan) is a different, sum-to-output notion.
Post-hoc rationalization: no formal definition found; only verbal accounts (report not causally upstream of the answer; 'causal bypassing', cited in the map as Morris & Plunkett 2025).
Plausibility as the contrast to faithfulness: no formal definition found (Jacovi & Goldberg 2021 separate causal from social attribution only semi-formally).

Simulatability: only informal definitions (Lipton 2016; Doshi-Velez & Kim 2017; Hase & Bansal 2020) plus metrics already in the map; Dasgupta et al.'s consistency as decoder accuracy is the closest formal analogue.

Introspection: no fully mathematical definition; the criteria are verbal-causal (Comsa & Shanahan, Lindsey) or resource-relative (Song et al.), and Lindsey's metacognitive-representation criterion is not operationalized.
